summary: When Jesus frees a blind and mute man, the leaders claim He casts out demons by Beelzebub; Jesus exposes the charge and warns of unforgivable blasphemy.
key_insight: Mark adds one short line that explains Jesus’ warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit: “because they said, ‘He has an unclean spirit.’ ” The leaders looked straight at the Spirit’s work in Jesus and called it Satan’s.
story: Jesus went into a house, and again such a crowd gathered that He and His disciples could not even eat bread. When His own people heard about it, they went out to take hold of Him, for they said, “He is out of His mind.” {Mk}
Then a man was brought to Him who was demon-possessed, blind and mute. Jesus healed him, so that he both spoke and saw. The crowds were amazed and said, “Could this be the Son of David?” {Mt}

But the Pharisees {Mt} and the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem {Mk} had another explanation: “This fellow does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, the ruler of the demons.” {Mt} Others, testing Him, demanded a sign from heaven. {Lk}

Jesus knew their thoughts. He called them to Himself and spoke to them in parables: {Mk} “How can Satan cast out Satan?” A kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, and neither can a divided house. If Satan has risen up against himself, he is finished. {Mk} And if Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom did their own sons cast them out? “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you.” {Mt}

“No one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man.” When a stronger one comes upon him and overcomes him, he takes away the armor the strong man trusted in and divides his spoils. {Lk} “He who is not with Me is against Me, and he who does not gather with Me scatters abroad.” {Mt}

Then Jesus gave a solemn warning: “Assuredly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the sons of men, and whatever blasphemies they may utter; but he who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is subject to eternal condemnation.” {Mk} A word spoken against the Son of Man could be forgiven, but not speaking against the Holy Spirit, either in this age or in the age to come. {Mt} He said this because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.” {Mk}

A tree is known by its fruit, He went on. “Brood of vipers! How can you, being evil, speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” Every idle word will be accounted for on the day of judgment. “For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” {Mt}
differences: Matthew says the man was blind and mute; Luke mentions only that the demon was mute. Mark does not describe the healing.
The accusers are “the Pharisees” in Matthew, “the scribes who came down from Jerusalem” in Mark, and “some of them” in the crowd in Luke.
Only Mark tells of Jesus’ family setting out to take hold of Him, and only Mark explains the warning about blasphemy by what the scribes were saying.

Matthew has “by the Spirit of God”; Luke has “with the finger of God.” Luke pictures the strong man “fully armed” and a stronger one taking his armor. Matthew alone adds the sayings about trees, fruit and careless words.
Matthew and Mark set this scene in Galilee before the parables by the sea; Luke tells it later, during Jesus’ journey toward Jerusalem (Luke 11).

fit.question: Matthew and Mark set this controversy in Galilee, shortly before the parables by the sea. Luke tells it in chapter 11, during Jesus’ later travels. Did it happen once or twice?

points.label: Luke groups teaching
points.text: Luke 9:51–19:27 follows Jesus toward Jerusalem, but it gathers much of His teaching by subject rather than by date. Luke may have placed this controversy among other teaching on prayer, light and hypocrisy because it belongs there in meaning.

points.label: A charge made more than once
points.text: The accusation came up often. Matthew records it after an earlier healing of a mute man (Matthew 9:34), and Jesus refers to it when He sends out the Twelve (Matthew 10:25). A traveling teacher who met the same slander in different towns would answer it in much the same words.

fit.note: Whether this happened once or twice, each Gospel reports what Jesus truly said; neither option requires an error.
fit.short: Either Luke grouped this teaching by subject, or Jesus answered the same charge, which came up often, on another occasion.

scene.label: Beelzebub
scene.text: The name probably comes from Baal-Zebub, the god of the Philistine city of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2), whose name can mean lord of the flies. By Jesus’ day it had become a name for the prince of demons.

scene.label: From Jerusalem
scene.text: Mark says the scribes had come down from Jerusalem, the center of religious authority. Their verdict was not village gossip; it carried the weight of the capital.

scene.label: Jewish exorcists
scene.text: Some Jews of the time did practice exorcism (Acts 19:13). Jesus asks why the leaders accepted their own exorcists but called His work Satan’s. The Gospels show Jesus using no rituals or incantations, only His word.

scene.label: The finger of God
scene.text: Luke’s phrase recalls Egypt, where Pharaoh’s magicians admitted, “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:19). Jesus’ power over demons was as plainly God’s as the plagues had been.

scene.label: The strong man
scene.text: Isaiah 49:24–25 asks whether captives can be taken from the mighty, and God answers that He Himself will contend with the oppressor and save His people. Jesus speaks of Himself as the one who binds the strong man and sets his captives free.

witnesses.matthew: Begins with the healing and the crowd’s question, “Could this be the Son of David?”, so the leaders’ charge answers a rising hope that Jesus is the promised King. Matthew alone adds the words about trees, fruit and careless words, turning the warning back on the accusers’ own speech.
witnesses.mark: Shows how hard-pressed Jesus was: no time to eat, and His own people saying He was out of His mind. Mark records the strongest words of warning, that the one who blasphemes the Spirit “is subject to eternal condemnation,” and he ties them directly to what the scribes said.
witnesses.luke: Sets the charge on the journey toward Jerusalem and links it to the demand for a sign, which Jesus answers a few verses later. His “finger of God” recalls the Exodus, and his picture of a stronger one dividing the spoils shows Jesus as the victor who frees Satan’s captives.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the stronger One who has entered the strong man’s house. Every demon He drove out was a sign that God’s kingdom had arrived and Satan’s hold was breaking.
seeing.living: Jesus leaves no neutral ground: “He who is not with Me is against Me.” Those who fear they have committed the unforgivable sin are not the ones Jesus warned; the danger is for those who see His work plainly and call it evil. Answer what He has done with thanks, and watch your words, for they show what fills the heart.
seeing.ponder: When you see the clear work of God, is your first response to welcome it or to explain it away?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus has bound the strong man; to call His work evil is to refuse the only Savior.
outline: The sin that shuts out forgiveness (28–30)
preaching.watch_for: Mark wraps the scribes’ charge (3:22–30) inside the story of Jesus’ family (3:20–21, 31–35). Both misjudge Him: the family says He is out of His mind, and the scribes say He is possessed.
